overview: Mapuche communities have histories of local autonomy, exchange and adaptation across southern South America. Their cultural life continued through colonial encounters and republican dispossession.

items.text: The lof organized related families. Local longko exercised limited authority; wartime alliances did not imply one permanent ruler over all communities.
Longko allocated fields among families and could reassign exhausted plots while they recovered. Community reserves provided additional access.
Seventeenth-century frontier commerce and movement toward the Pampas transformed family and economic relationships.
Manuel Manquilef's writings and Pascual Coña's narrated life offer Mapuche perspectives on historical change.
Nineteenth-century Chilean and Argentine campaigns occupied Mapuche territories. Restricted lands and later urban migration transformed communities without ending Mapuche identity.
